# **Assumption Prioritization Canvas: How to Identify And Test The Right Assumptions**

# 

# ---

# **In product management, [most of our ideas are not going to work](https://www.productcompass.pm/i/89380899/why-do-we-need-product-discovery).**

# **It’s essential to test our assumptions before the implementation.**

# **But you can’t test everything. And you can’t test what you’re unaware of.**

# **So, in today’s newsletter, I want to explain how to identify and test the right assumptions:**

1. # **Traditional Assumptions Mapping Techniques**

2. # **The Assumption Prioritization Canvas**

3. # **How to Identify Hidden Assumptions**

4. # **Summary and Takeaways**

# **Let’s dive into it right now.**

## **1\. Traditional Assumptions Mapping Techniques**

# **The original Assumptions Mapping technique was developed by Jeff Gothelf and Josh Seiden, co-authors of [Lean UX](https://res.productcompass.pm/top-product-management-books/lean-ux).**

# **David Bland, co-author of [Testing Business Ideas](https://res.productcompass.pm/top-product-management-books/testing-business-ideas) (from Strategyzer), who worked with them, developed his own approach.**

# **The goal of both techniques is to identify and test the riskiest assumptions before the implementation.**

# **But the details of the two approaches differ significantly.**

# **Let’s break them down with some critical comments.**

### **1.1 Assumptions Mapping by David Bland (Strategyzer)**

# **Strategyzer’s approach aims to answer the question, “Which assumptions to test.”**

# **Each assumption represents an identified risk. Let me [quote three main risk areas](https://www.strategyzer.com/library/how-assumptions-mapping-can-focus-your-teams-on-running-experiments-that-matter) suggested by David Bland:**

* # **Desirability: Does the market want this idea?**

* # **Feasibility: Can we deliver at scale?**

* # **Viability: Is the idea profitable enough?**

# **While David emphasizes a cross-functional collaboration, [according to him](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PyCvsBrKO4w):**

* # **Desirability risk is primarily the responsibility of Designers, not Product Managers.**

* # **Feasibility risk is primarily the responsibility of Engineers.**

* # **Viability risk is primarily the responsibility of the Product Manager.**

# **Steps you take in order to identify and perform the right experiments:**

# **Step 1: Create a [Business Model Canvas](https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1hgz250jgK4TXIDoPQFoomRNW5cWtV8Q2/edit?usp=sharing&ouid=111307342557889008106&rtpof=true&sd=true) and (later) a [Value Proposition Canvas](https://www.strategyzer.com/library/the-value-proposition-canvas) if you haven’t already.**

# **Step 2: Write down assumptions related to Desirability, Viability, and Feasibility. You can use sticky notes and place them around the canvases:**

# **![Identify Hypotheses by Strategyzer][image1]**

# **Adapted by Paweł Huryn from an image by [Strategyzer](https://www.strategyzer.com/library/how-assumptions-mapping-can-focus-your-teams-on-running-experiments-that-matter)**

# [**On his website**](https://www.precoil.com/resources)**, David Bland has also shared a [list of questions](https://www.dropbox.com/s/qfomji91krnho0j/Assumptions%20Mapping%20Worksheet%20-%20Precoil%20v3.0.pdf?dl=0) you can ask yourself when mapping assumptions.**

# **Step 3: For each assumption, assess its importance and how much evidence you have.**

# **Next, focus your experiments on the top right corner, share assumptions in the left-right corner with your team (and internal stakeholders), and defer testing everything else:**

# **![Assumption Mapping 2x2 Diagram by Strategyzer][image2]**

# **Adapted from an image by [Strategyzer](https://www.strategyzer.com/library/how-assumptions-mapping-can-focus-your-teams-on-running-experiments-that-matter)**

# **Step 4: Perform an experiment to test the riskiest assumption(s), learn from it, and repeat. It’s an iterative process.**

#### **Assumptions mapping by David Bland (Strategyzer): A critical look**

# **While I love the Strategyzer book series, I have a few doubts related to the 2x2 Diagram and their recommended workflow.**

# **It’s clear to me that David’s Assumptions Mapping was highly influenced by Design Thinking and long-term research projects performed primarily by UX Researchers.**

# **But the notion that Designers own the entire Desirability risk contradicts the responsibilities explained by Marty Cagan in [Inspired](https://res.productcompass.pm/top-product-management-books/inspired), where:**

* # **The Product Manager focuses on Value risk,**

* # **The Product Designer focuses on Usability risk.**

# **It also doesn’t match how most product teams work. In my experience, and I discussed it with hundreds of professionals, while Product Discovery is teamwork, it’s usually the PM who leads and facilitates the discovery.**

# **Also, David's approach focuses on working with new products (aka Product Innovation or [Initial Product Discovery](https://www.productcompass.pm/i/89380899/what-is-initial-product-discovery)).**

# **I'd argue that it’s not well-adjusted to [Continuous Product Discovery](https://www.productcompass.pm/i/89380899/whats-inside-continuous-product-discovery), where you do not start with the Business Model.**

# **Another issue is that summarizing Desirability risk as “Does the market want this idea?” might not be clear enough for product teams.**

# **Why?**

# **Imagine you created a landing page to validate the market engagement by collecting preorders. The fact that the market wants your idea doesn’t mean users will figure out how to use it. It doesn't mean that the idea will actually deliver the value promised as part of your [Value Proposition](https://www.productcompass.pm/p/how-to-design-value-proposition-template). And it doesn’t mean you know how to market that idea (Go-to-Market).**

# **While theoretically, you can collect all those questions under the “Desirability” umbrella (and David does this), people might not remember to ask those questions.**

# **For all those reasons, I prefer:**

* # **Marty Cagan’s Value, Usability, Viability, and Feasibility risks for existing products.**

* # **Add a Go-to-Market risk as a separate category for new initiatives.**

# **I explained this, together with the extended risk classification in [How to Manage Risks as a Product Manager](https://www.productcompass.pm/p/how-to-manage-risks-as-a-product-manager).**

# **Finally, while the horizontal axis (the amount of evidence) is clear, the “Importance” is ambiguous. What does it mean for an assumption to be important? Some might assume it’s related to Risk, but in Jeff Gothelf’s approach (from which it was adapted), the Risk is on the horizontal axis.**

# **The framework should clarify how to interpret the labels to streamline the communication.**

### **1.2 Assumptions Mapping by Jeff Gothelf (Hypothesis Prioritization Canvas)**

# **What’s different about Jeff’s canvas (the original one that David adapted):**

* # **It answers two questions, not one:**

  * # **Which assumptions to test,**

  * # **Which ideas to build.**

* # **It assesses the “Risk” instead of the “Amount of evidence.” This is not the same. The risk involves both probability (related but not the same as the amount of evidence) and effort (negative consequences in the form of waste if the risk materializes).**

* # **It assesses a correlated “Value” (of building a product of a feature) instead of the “Importance” of an assumption.**

# **A free template:**

# **![Source & template: The Hypothesis Prioritization Canvas by Jeff Gothelf][image3]**

# **Source & template: [The Hypothesis Prioritization Canvas by Jeff Gothelf](https://jeffgothelf.com/blog/the-hypothesis-prioritization-canvas/)**

#### **Assumptions mapping by Jeff Gothelf: A critical look**

# **First, none of my doubts about David Bland’s framework apply to Jeff Gothelf’s approach.**

# **The [Lean UX](https://res.productcompass.pm/top-product-management-books/lean-ux), a fantastic book Jeff co-authored, perfectly explains the workflow. In particular:**

* # **It emphasizes the importance of cross-functional research and discovery but doesn’t specify how competencies in the team relate to specific risk areas.**

* # **It doesn’t even mention a specific risk taxonomy. It gives you the freedom to classify the risks how you want.**

* # **It emphasizes the importance of Continuous Product Discovery and explains how to integrate assumptions mapping practices with Agile and Scrum.**

# **What I also like is that Hypothesis Prioritization Canvas uses unambiguous labels on the axes.**

# **At the same time, here are a few details I’d like to improve:**

* # **We build ideas, not assumptions. And we have [better ways of prioritizing ideas](https://www.productcompass.pm/p/prioritization-framework-product-backlog). Thus, I'd like to focus on answering which assumptions are worth testing.**

* # **I’d like to explain what the risk is for those who might struggle with the term.**

* # **I’d like to recommend risk topologies and questions to ask depending on the discovery type (new vs. existing products).**

* # **I’d like to demonstrate how to combine Jeff Gothelf's prioritization with the [RICE/ICE](https://www.productcompass.pm/i/95087405/prioritization-templates) scoring so that it works with other techniques.**

## **2\. The Assumption Prioritization Canvas**

# **Let’s look at the Assumption Prioritization Canvas, which combines elements of the two approaches:**

# **![Assumption Prioritization Canvas, Assumption Mapping][image4]**

# [**Assumption Prioritization Canvas**](https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1Npnm75WMHma0a75THZvbP0d0aLOkLwGB/edit?usp=sharing&ouid=111307342557889008106&rtpof=true&sd=true) **by Paweł Huryn**

# [Download template (File \> Download)](https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1Npnm75WMHma0a75THZvbP0d0aLOkLwGB/edit?usp=sharing&ouid=111307342557889008106&rtpof=true&sd=true)

# **The key changes made compared to the Hypothesis Prioritization Canvas:**

* # **It focuses on which assumptions to test because we can’t indicate whether we should build an idea just by looking at a single assumption.**

* # **It clarifies that Risk \= (1 \- Confidence) \* Effort, where Confidence and Effort are known from [RICE/ICE](https://www.productcompass.pm/i/95087405/prioritization-templates). This helps you use assumptions mapping together with popular [idea prioritization techniques](https://www.productcompass.pm/p/prioritization-framework-product-backlog).**

* # **The term “Value” was replaced with “Impact,” known from ICE. This emphasizes the importance of including not just the value you can create but also the number of customers affected.**

* # **It explains when it makes sense to run tiny experiments (low cost and short time.**

# **As a rule of thumb, each experiment shifts your assumptions to the left but can also influence the estimated Impact and Risk as you learn more.**

# [Share](https://www.productcompass.pm/p/assumption-prioritization-canvas?utm_source=substack&utm_medium=email&utm_content=share&action=share)

### **2.1 How to use the Assumption Prioritization Canvas**

# **The entire cross-functional team (aka the “Product Trio”) must work together.**

# **It typically includes a Product Manager, Designer, and at least one Engineer. While everyone has unique core competencies, there are no silos, and anyone can contribute to any risk area. For more information, see [Product Trio: Beyond the Obvious](https://www.productcompass.pm/p/product-trio).**

# **Whether you are performing [Continuous or Initial Product Discovery](https://www.productcompass.pm/p/what-exactly-is-product-discovery), your team needs to:**

1. # **Start with a clear goal, either in pursuit of the Product-Market Fit or a meaningful problem to solve with clear desired outcomes. For more information, see [Business Outcomes vs Product Outcomes vs Customer Outcomes](https://www.productcompass.pm/p/business-outcomes-vs-product-outcomes) and [Product Team Principles from TRANSFORMED](https://www.productcompass.pm/p/product-model-first-principles-transformed-cagan).**

2. # **Explore the problem space (e.g., customer interviews, data analytics, market research, interviewing stakeholders).**

3. # **Define your knowledge about the specific problems you are going to tackle ([Opportunities](https://www.productcompass.pm/i/89380899/whats-inside-continuous-product-discovery) or [Jobs-to-be-Done](https://www.productcompass.pm/p/jobs-to-be-done-masterclass-with)). A common approach when working with existing products is using the [Opportunity Solution Tree](https://www.productcompass.pm/i/89380899/whats-inside-continuous-product-discovery).**

4. # **Ideate on how you can solve those problems and prioritize those ideas based on the Opportunity Score and other factors (e.g., value for the business). A simple approach that can aggregate different factors is ICE scoring. I explained this in [How to Prioritize Ideas as a Product Manager](https://www.productcompass.pm/p/prioritization-framework-product-backlog),**

5. # **Identify assumptions related to Value, Usability, Viability, and Feasibility risks for an existing product. For a new product, consider also the Go-to-Market risk. I presented detailed questions you can ask for each risk category in [the extended risk classification](https://www.productcompass.pm/p/how-to-manage-risks-as-a-product-manager). An excerpt:**

6. # [**![The extended product risk classification][image5]**](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!W5Ub!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F3f330dbc-b47d-446d-ba70-a8eece5c1133_1155x689.png)

7. # [**The extended product risk classification**](https://www.productcompass.pm/p/how-to-manage-risks-as-a-product-manager) **(excerpt)**

8. # **Test: Focus on testing the riskiest assumption first. As a rule of thumb, conduct 1-2 experiments at a time. Learn from it and repeat. It’s a continuous, non-linear process.**

# **Once there are no more assumptions to be tested, you can select an idea for implementation \- Product Discovery results in a validated product backlog.**

# **The entire workflow ([the Double Diamond of Product Discovery and the Triple Diamond of Product Management](https://www.productcompass.pm/p/the-double-diamond-of-design-thinking)) can be visualized as:**

## **3\. How to Identify Hidden Assumptions**

# **You can't prioritize and test what you are unaware of. I recommend two ways of identifying hidden assumptions.**

### **3.1 User Story Map**

# **One of the best ways to identify assumptions related to Value, Usability, and Feasibility is to use the User Story Map.**

# **Identify the steps a user takes to derive value from your product and consider the three risk areas for each step.**

# **I also include system steps to help identify Feasibility risks easily.**

## **4\. Summary and Takeaways**

# **In product management, most of our ideas are not going to work.**

# **It’s essential to test our assumptions before the implementation. But you can’t test everything, and you can’t test what you’re unaware of.**

## **Part 1: The Basics**

**![][image9]**

### **1.1 History of Estimation Questions in Product Management**

Estimation questions, perhaps obviously to some, have their roots in **management consulting**. But over time, they've made their way **squarely into the tech industry**, *particularly for product management (PM) roles*.

The shift towards more structured estimation questions for PMs began in the **late 1990s and early 2000s**, coinciding with the dot-com boom. As tech companies grew rapidly, they needed a way to assess candidates' ability to think analytically about product-related challenges.

Companies like **Google** and **Amazon** were the early adopters, adapting estimation techniques to focus on user behavior, market size for new products, and potential impact of product decisions.

These questions were designed to assess not just analytical skills, but also creativity and the ability to work with limited information \- qualities essential for product managers in fast-paced tech environments.

By the **2010s**, estimation questions **had become a** **staple** in PM interviews across various tech companies. Facebook (now Meta), Apple, and countless startups incorporated these questions into their hiring processes for product roles.

The evolution of estimation questions for PMs reflects the changing nature of product management:

* **Early tech adopters** used them to test analytical rigor and market understanding.  
* As data became more central to product decisions, questions evolved to assess a candidate's **ability to work with metrics** and make data-driven decisions.  
* Modern tech companies use them to evaluate a candidate's ability to think about **scale**, understand user behavior, and **estimate the impact of product changes**.

Today, estimation questions are a core part of many PM interview processes.

They've evolved from simple market sizing exercises to complex scenarios that might involve user engagement metrics, feature adoption rates, or revenue projections for new products.

As we move into the 2020s, with the rise of AI and big data, estimation questions for PMs are evolving once again.

They're now often used to assess a candidate's ability to think about personalization at scale, understand the implications of machine learning on product metrics, and consider the ethical implications of product decisions.

*Understanding this history not only gives you context but also helps you appreciate why these questions are asked and what interviewers are really looking for.*

### **1.2 Most Common Users of Estimation Questions in Tech**

The use of estimation questions spans various roles in the tech industry, each adapting the technique to its specific needs.

In product management, companies like Google, Facebook (Meta), Amazon, and Apple use these questions to assess a candidate's ability to think about product metrics, user behavior, and market opportunities.

They're looking for PMs who can make data-driven decisions and estimate the impact of product changes.

Each of the tech giants have their own spin:

* [Google](https://www.news.aakashg.com/i/137367780/the-google-pm-interview-guide) might ask you to estimate the number of Gmail users who would adopt a new feature.  
* [Meta](https://www.news.aakashg.com/p/meta-pm-job) (Facebook) could ask about the potential engagement increase from a new News Feed algorithm.  
* [Apple](https://www.news.aakashg.com/i/137367780/the-apple-pm-interview-guide) could ask about the market size for a new wearable device.  
* Amazon might want you to estimate the impact on Prime subscriptions if they introduced a new benefit.

They might label them differently, but each is a flavor of Product Estimation question.

Even smaller tech companies and startups use these questions to evaluate a PM's ability to think about growth and scale.

Across the tech industry, certain roles are more likely to face these questions:

* Product Managers (obviously)  
* Growth Managers focusing on user acquisition and retention  
* Data Scientists working on product analytics  
* UX Researchers estimating user behavior changes  
* Marketing Managers, especially in product marketing roles

The key takeaway? If you're aiming for a product-related role in tech, being prepared for estimation questions isn't just helpful \- **it's essential**.

### **1.3 What do Estimation Questions Actually Test for PMs?**

At their heart, estimation questions probe for a set of core competencies crucial in product management roles. There’s 10 competency areas that fall into 3 buckets:

#### **The Core Competencies**

1. **Structured Thinking**  
   Interviewers watch how you organize your thoughts about user segments, feature adoption, or market opportunities.  
2. **Analytical Prowess**  
   Your ability to work with product metrics, make reasonable assumptions about user behavior, and perform quick calculations is under the microscope.  
3. **Product Sense**  
   These questions test your intuition about user needs, product-market fit, and how changes might impact user behavior.  
4. **Market Understanding**  
   Your grasp of the tech landscape, user trends, and potential opportunities comes into play.  
5. **Growth Mindset**  
   Can you think creatively about user acquisition, engagement, and retention strategies?

#### **Beyond the Numbers**

While quantitative skills are important, estimation questions for PMs dig deeper:

6. **Business Acumen**  
   Your understanding of how product decisions tie to business outcomes is crucial.  
7. **Comfort with Ambiguity**  
   In product management, you'll rarely have all the data you need. These questions test your ability to make progress with incomplete information.  
8. **Communication Skills**  
   Throughout the process, you're demonstrating your ability to articulate product strategies and data insights clearly.

#### **The Hidden Evaluations**

Some aspects of these questions are less obvious but equally important for PM roles:

9. **Stakeholder Management**  
   Can you defend your estimates and product decisions convincingly?  
10. **Cross-Functional Understanding**  
    Do your estimates and assumptions demonstrate an understanding of different aspects of the business (engineering constraints, marketing channels, etc.)?

It’s not like they are trying to concoct things to weed people out. The idea is to test skills that really matter to PMs.

# **Part 2: The Techniques**

*Now that we understand the basics, let's dive into the techniques to excel. This section will cover both **tried-and-true strategies** and some **unconventional approaches** to stand out.*

*![][image10]*

## **2.1 Principles \+ Frameworks**

The way to think about these questions is to have a foundational mental framework, and then know all the other frameworks and when to use them.

Here’s what you need to know.

### **The Foundation: GAME**

When tackling estimation questions as a PM, start with the GAME framework:

* **G**oals: Understand the product or feature objectives  
* **A**ssumptions: Make educated guesses about user behavior and market conditions  
* **M**etrics: Identify key performance indicators (KPIs) to measure  
* **E**stimate: Perform calculations based on your assumptions and metrics

This approach provides a solid foundation for most product-related estimation scenarios.

Then, pick and choose any other frameworks you need to add. The two most common one’s are for types of metrics (HEART) and funnels (AARRR):

### **Types of Metrics: HEART**

Google's HEART framework is useful for structuring product metrics:

* **H**appiness: User satisfaction and attitudes  
* **E**ngagement: Level of user involvement  
* **A**doption: New user acquisition  
* **R**etention: User churn rate  
* **T**ask success: Efficiency and effectiveness of user activities

Use this to ensure you're considering all aspects of product performance in your estimates.

### **Funnels: AARRR**

For questions about product growth and funnels, remember the AARRR framework:

* **A**cquisition: How users find your product  
* **A**ctivation: Users' first positive experience  
* **R**etention: Repeated product usage  
* **R**eferral: Users recommending your product  
* **R**evenue: Monetization of users

This helps structure your thinking about different stages of the user lifecycle.

Once you have the basic framework, consider a sanity check or scenario analysis.

### **Reality Checks and Scenarios**

Two complementary approaches can enhance your estimates:

#### **The Sanity Check Method**

Use known facts to verify your estimate's reasonableness. Start with a range: what's definitely too high or too low? This grounds your estimate in reality.

#### **The Scenario Analysis Approach**

Particularly useful for market sizing, this involves:

1. Identifying different user segments or scenarios  
2. Estimating each separately  
3. Combining for a total estimate

This nuanced approach demonstrates business acumen and attention to detail.

People love it.

### **Putting It All Together**

These frameworks are **tools, not rules**. The best approach often involves combining elements from multiple frameworks. With practice, you'll develop an intuition for which techniques work best for different types of questions.

In your preparations, try applying different frameworks to the same problem. This flexibility will serve you well in the dynamic environment of an interview.

### **2.2 Unconventional Techniques to Stand Out**

In today's competitive job market, standard frameworks aren't enough. You need to bring something extra to truly shine.

Let's explore some unconventional techniques that can set you apart.

#### **Differentiator 1 \- User Journey Mapping**

Instead of just crunching numbers, sketch out a quick user journey map. This visual aid helps both you and your interviewer follow your thought process about user behavior and potential drop-off points.

For example, when estimating the adoption rate of a new feature, map out the steps a user would take to discover, understand, and use the feature. This showcases your user-centric thinking \- a crucial PM skill.

#### **Differentiator 2 \- Visual Thinking**

Most candidates approach estimation questions verbally. But incorporating quick sketches or diagrams can make you stand out.

Imagine estimating the number of gas stations in a city. Quickly sketch out a city grid. This visual aid helps both you and your interviewer follow your thought process.

It also showcases your ability to communicate complex ideas visually. That's a valuable skill in many roles.

#### **Differentiator 3 \- Metric Correlation Analysis**

When estimating the impact on one metric, consider how it might affect others. This demonstrates systems thinking and a holistic view of product health.

For instance, if you're estimating an increase in user engagement, also consider how it might impact retention, monetization, or customer support load.

This approach shows you understand the interconnected nature of product metrics.

#### **Differentiator 4 \- Reversing the Question**

Try estimating the inverse of what's asked. This can provide valuable context and demonstrate flexible thinking.

Asked to estimate how many users will adopt a new feature? Also consider how many won't, and why. This helps identify potential barriers to adoption and shows strategic product thinking.

#### **Differentiator 5 \- Incorporating Future Trends**

Weave predictions about future tech trends into your estimation. It shows you're forward-thinking and aware of the broader tech landscape.

Estimating the market for a new device? Consider how emerging technologies like AR or 5G might impact adoption rates in the coming years.

This demonstrates proactivity in staying informed \- a crucial trait for PMs who need to anticipate market changes.

You don’t need to use each differentiator in each interview. But dropping one into each interview usually is wise.

### **2.3 How to Avoid the Most Common Mistakes Candidates Make**

So that’s *what to do*. What about *what not to do?*

In coaching candidates, I’ve found that even well-prepared candidates can fall into common traps. Being aware of these pitfalls can help you navigate around them.

![][image11]

#### **Mistake 1 \- Rushing to a Number**

One of the biggest mistakes is hurrying to provide an answer. This can lead to skipping crucial steps or making unfounded assumptions.

Take your time to structure your approach. Explain your thinking clearly. Interviewers care more about your process than the final number.

#### **Mistake 2 \- Failing to State Assumptions**

Every estimation requires assumptions. Articulating these clearly is crucial.

Don't just pull numbers out of thin air. Explain why you chose those specific values. This demonstrates thoughtfulness and attention to detail.

#### **Mistake 3 \- Skipping the Sanity Check**

Many candidates forget to step back and assess their final answer. Always ask yourself if your estimate seems reasonable.

If you've concluded there are more cars than people in a city, something has probably gone wrong. Catching and correcting such errors shows self-awareness and critical thinking.

#### **Mistake 4 \- Ignoring Segmentation**

Not all users or customers are the same. Treating them as a homogeneous group can lead to inaccurate estimates.

Consider different segments. Think about how they might affect your calculations. This nuanced approach demonstrates business acumen.

#### **Mistake 5 \- Ignoring Business Goals**

Some candidates get caught up in product features without tying them back to business objectives.

How to avoid it: Begin your estimation by clarifying the business goal. Is it user growth? Revenue increase? Cost reduction? Make sure your approach aligns with this goal.

#### **Mistake 6 \- Being Too Rigid**

Frameworks are helpful, but don't be afraid to adapt or combine them as needed.

Flexibility in your thinking is valuable. It shows you can handle complex, ambiguous problems \- a key skill in many roles.

By avoiding these common mistakes and incorporating unconventional techniques, you'll be well-equipped to tackle even the toughest estimation questions.

In our next section, we'll dive into specific examples. We'll walk through how to approach different types of estimation questions step-by-step.

## **Part 3: Question Response Examples**

Now that we've covered the techniques and common pitfalls, let's dive into some real-world examples.

We'll walk through 1 example from each category of estimation question you can expect, and then give you homework to practice 10 more questions:

1. User Engagement  
2. Feature Impact  
3. Monetization  
4. Performance and Scale  
5. Retention and Satisfaction  
6. Market Sizing

### **1\. User Engagement**

#### **Example: What's the expected increase in user engagement if we implement a personalized recommendation system?**

**Candidate**: Before we dive into the estimation, I'd like to clarify the type of business we're dealing with. Could you provide some context about our platform?

**Interviewer**: We're a streaming video platform, similar to YouTube. Our main goal with the recommendation system is to increase watch time and user retention.

**Candidate**: Thank you for that context. Given that we're a streaming video platform, let's consider several potential engagement metrics we could focus on, along with their pros and cons:

1. **Average Watch Time per User per Day**  
   Pros:  
   • Directly aligns with our goal of increasing watch time  
   • Comprehensive measure of engagement (frequency and duration)  
   • Easy to track and compare before and after implementation  
   Cons:  
   • Doesn't capture the quality of engagement  
   • May not reflect improvements in content discovery if users watch fewer, longer videos  
2. **Videos Watched per Session**  
   Pros:  
   • Indicates improved content discovery  
   • Easy to measure and understand  
   Cons:  
   • Doesn't account for video length  
   • May decrease if users find more relevant, longer-form content  
3. **7-day or 30-day Retention Rate**  
   Pros:  
   • Directly measures our retention goal  
   • Indicates long-term engagement and user satisfaction  
   Cons:  
   • Takes longer to measure impact  
   • May be influenced by factors other than recommendations  
4. **Click-through Rate (CTR) on Recommended Videos**  
   Pros:  
   • Directly measures the effectiveness of recommendations  
   • Quick to show results after implementation  
   Cons:  
   • Doesn't capture engagement beyond the initial click  
   • May encourage clickbait-style recommendations  
5. **Average Session Duration**  
   Pros:  
   • Indicates user satisfaction and content relevance  
   • Likely to increase with better recommendations  
   Cons:  
   • Doesn't capture frequency of engagement  
   • May not increase if users find content more efficiently  
6. **Daily Active Users (DAU)**  
   Pros:  
   • Measures overall platform engagement  
   • Indicates if recommendations are bringing users back more often  
   Cons:  
   • Doesn't capture depth of engagement  
   • May be influenced by factors beyond recommendations

Considering our goals of increasing watch time and user retention, I propose we focus on "Average Watch Time per User per Day" as our primary engagement metric. It directly aligns with our watch time goal, provides a comprehensive view of engagement, and should reflect improvements in both content relevance and user retention.

However, I would also suggest monitoring CTR on recommended videos and 30-day retention rate as secondary metrics to get a more complete picture of the recommendation system's impact.

Would you agree with this approach, or would you prefer to focus on a different metric?

**Interviewer**: Your analysis makes sense. Let's proceed with Average Watch Time per User per Day as our primary metric.

**Candidate**: Great, thank you. Now, to estimate the impact on Average Watch Time per User per Day, we'll need some baseline data. The key variables I'd want to know are:

1. Current average watch time per user per day  
2. Percentage of watch time currently driven by recommendations  
3. Average session duration  
4. Current time spent browsing for content

Do we have this data available, or would you like me to make some assumptions?

**Interviewer**: Let's work with assumptions for now.

**Candidate**: Understood. Let's assume:

1. Current average watch time: 30 minutes per user per day  
2. 20% of watch time currently comes from recommended videos  
3. Average session duration: 15 minutes  
4. Users currently spend an average of 5 minutes per day browsing for content

Now, let's estimate how a personalized recommendation system might impact these:

1. **Improved relevance**: Better recommendations should increase the percentage of watch time from recommended videos. Let's estimate this could increase from 20% to 25-35%.  
2. **Reduced browsing time**: More relevant recommendations might reduce time spent browsing. Let's estimate a potential decrease of 20-40% in browsing time.  
3. **Potential negative impact**: Some users might feel the recommendations are limiting their discovery, potentially reducing their overall engagement. Let's estimate this might affect 5-15% of users, reducing their watch time by 10-20%.

So we can calculate three scenarios:

Conservative Scenario:

* Recommendation watch time increases to 25%: 30 min \* (1 \+ (0.25 \- 0.2)) \= 31.5 min  
* 20% decrease in browsing time: 5 min \* 0.8 \= 4 min saved  
* 5% of users reduce watch time by 10%: 31.5 min \* 0.95 \+ 31.5 min \* 0.05 \* 0.9 \= 31.34 min  
* Total: 31.34 min \+ 4 min \= 35.34 min

Moderate Scenario:

* Recommendation watch time increases to 30%: 30 min \* (1 \+ (0.3 \- 0.2)) \= 33 min  
* 30% decrease in browsing time: 5 min \* 0.7 \= 3.5 min saved  
* 10% of users reduce watch time by 15%: 33 min \* 0.9 \+ 33 min \* 0.1 \* 0.85 \= 32.51 min  
* Total: 32.51 min \+ 3.5 min \= 36.01 min

Optimistic Scenario:

* Recommendation watch time increases to 35%: 30 min \* (1 \+ (0.35 \- 0.2)) \= 34.5 min  
* 40% decrease in browsing time: 5 min \* 0.6 \= 3 min saved  
* 5% of users reduce watch time by 10%: 34.5 min \* 0.95 \+ 34.5 min \* 0.05 \* 0.9 \= 34.33 min  
* Total: 34.33 min \+ 3 min \= 37.33 min

Based on this analysis, I estimate that implementing a personalized recommendation system could increase our average watch time per user per day from 30 minutes to between 35.34 and 37.33 minutes, with a moderate estimate of 36.01 minutes. The moderate estimate represents roughly a 20% increase.

Does this look reasonable to you \- are there any other factors you think we should consider?

#### **Why it Works**

This answer effectively uses GAME to clarify the goals, asks about assumptions, strategically chooses metrics, and then actually follows through on an estimation.

On top of that, it uses scenario analysis to create a differentiator from other candidates.

Along the way, it demonstrates all 10 core competencies companies are looking for.

It’s the perfect example of the type of response you should aim for.

#### **Additional Practice Questions:**

1. How might implementing a "quick view" feature impact the average number of products viewed per session in our e-commerce app?  
2. What could be the effect on average lesson completion rate if we introduce an adaptive learning algorithm in our online course platform?  
3. How might adding a "related articles" section impact the average number of articles read per visit on our news website?  
4. What engagement changes could we expect in terms of average workout duration if we implement a virtual coaching feature in our fitness app?  
5. How might introducing a "collaborative playlist" feature affect the average listening time per user in our music streaming app?  
6. What could be the impact on average task completion time if we add an AI-powered suggestion feature to our project management tool?  
7. How might implementing a "daily challenge" feature affect the average number of games played per day in our mobile puzzle game?  
8. What engagement changes could we expect in terms of average message response time if we introduce smart reply suggestions in our messaging app?  
9. How might adding a "skill endorsement" feature impact the average number of profile views per user in our professional networking platform?  
10. What could be the effect on average transaction frequency if we implement a personalized offer system in our mobile banking app?

## **2\. Feature Impact and Product Changes**

### **Example: How many customer support tickets might we receive if we launch a new feature to our existing user base?**

**Candidate**: Before we dive into the estimation, I'd like to clarify some details about the new feature and our user base. Could you provide some context about the feature we're launching and our current customer base size?

**Interviewer**: We're launching a new video editing tool within our social media app. Our current active user base is about 10 million monthly active users.

**Candidate**: Thank you for that context. To estimate the number of customer support tickets we might receive, let's consider several factors that could influence ticket volume:

1. User Adoption Rate  
   * How many users are likely to try the new feature?  
   * How quickly will adoption spread?  
2. Feature Complexity  
   * How intuitive is the video editing tool?  
   * Are there any complex operations that might confuse users?  
3. Existing Support Infrastructure  
   * What's our current ticket volume?  
   * How does it typically change with new feature launches?  
4. User Demographics  
   * Are our users generally tech-savvy?  
   * Do we have segments that might struggle more with new features?  
5. Launch Communication  
   * How well will we explain the new feature to users?  
   * Will we provide in-app tutorials or guides?

To structure our estimation, let's use a customer journey map approach to identify potential sources of support tickets:

1. **Discovery**: Users learn about the new feature  
   * Confusion about feature availability  
   * Questions about feature capabilities  
2. **First Use**: Users try the feature for the first time  
   * Difficulty finding or accessing the feature  
   * Issues with UI/UX navigation  
3. **Basic Usage**: Users start editing videos  
   * Questions about basic editing functions  
   * Problems with video import/export  
4. **Advanced Usage**: Users explore more complex editing options  
   * Inquiries about advanced features  
   * Troubleshooting for specific editing techniques  
5. **Sharing**: Users attempt to share their edited videos  
   * Issues with video quality or format  
   * Problems with sharing to different platforms

Now, let's estimate the ticket volume based on this journey. I'll need some baseline data. Do we have information on:

1. Our current daily support ticket volume?  
2. The percentage increase in tickets we typically see with new feature launches?  
3. The expected adoption rate for this feature in the first month?

**Interviewer**: Let's work with assumptions for those numbers.

**Candidate**: Understood. I'll make some reasonable assumptions based on industry standards and the information provided:

1. Current daily support ticket volume: 1,000 tickets (0.01% of our 10 million MAU)  
2. Typical increase in tickets with new features: 20-30%  
3. Expected adoption rate in the first month: 10-20% of our user base

Let's break down the additional tickets we might receive in the first month by journey stage:

**Conservative Scenario (10% adoption rate: 1,000,000 users try the feature):**

1. Discovery: 0.1% of users \= 1,000 tickets  
2. First Use: 0.3% of users \= 3,000 tickets  
3. Basic Usage: 0.4% of users \= 4,000 tickets  
4. Advanced Usage: 0.1% of users \= 1,000 tickets  
5. Sharing: 0.1% of users \= 1,000 tickets  
6. Total: 10,000 additional tickets (1% of users who try the feature)  
7. Daily increase: \~333 additional tickets per day (33% increase)

**Moderate Scenario (15% adoption rate: 1,500,000 users try the feature):**

1. Discovery: 0.15% of users \= 2,250 tickets  
2. First Use: 0.45% of users \= 6,750 tickets  
3. Basic Usage: 0.6% of users \= 9,000 tickets  
4. Advanced Usage: 0.15% of users \= 2,250 tickets  
5. Sharing: 0.15% of users \= 2,250 tickets  
6. Total: 22,500 additional tickets (1.5% of users who try the feature)  
7. Daily increase: \~750 additional tickets per day (75% increase)

**Optimistic Scenario (20% adoption rate: 2,000,000 users try the feature):**

1. Discovery: 0.08% of users \= 1,600 tickets  
2. First Use: 0.24% of users \= 4,800 tickets  
3. Basic Usage: 0.32% of users \= 6,400 tickets  
4. Advanced Usage: 0.08% of users \= 1,600 tickets  
5. Sharing: 0.08% of users \= 1,600 tickets  
6. Total: 16,000 additional tickets (0.8% of users who try the feature)  
7. Daily increase: \~533 additional tickets per day (53% increase)

Based on this analysis, I estimate that launching the new video editing feature could increase our daily support ticket volume by 333 to 750 tickets, with a moderate estimate of about 750 additional tickets per day. This represents a 33% to 75% increase in our daily ticket volume.

Insights from the journey-based breakdown:

1. First Use and Basic Usage stages are likely to generate the most tickets, as users familiarize themselves with the new interface and functionality.  
2. Advanced Usage and Sharing stages generate fewer tickets but may require more complex support.  
3. The Discovery stage generates the least tickets but may indicate areas where we can improve our feature introduction and user education.

**Sanity Check**: Let's compare this to our typical increase of 20-30% for new features. Our estimate is higher, which makes sense given that this is a complex feature (video editing) that might be challenging for some users. The estimated 0.8-1.5% of users submitting tickets also seems reasonable for a new, potentially complex feature.

Is there any part of this estimation you'd like me to expand on or reconsider?

### **Why it Works**

This answer effectively uses the GAME framework and then demonstrates thoughtful analysis by:

1. Using a customer journey map to identify potential ticket sources  
2. Considering multiple factors that could influence ticket volume  
3. Providing conservative, moderate, and optimistic scenarios  
4. Performing a sanity check against typical metrics

This approach showcases analytical thinking, problem-solving skills, and business acumen \- all valuable traits for product managers.

## **3\. Revenue and Monetization**

### **Example: If we introduce a freemium model for our SaaS product, what percentage of free users might convert to paid users in the first six months?**

**Candidate**: Before we dive into the estimation, I'd like to clarify some details about our SaaS product and the planned freemium model. Could you provide some context about our product, target market, and the key differences between the free and paid tiers?

**Interviewer**: Our product is a project management tool primarily aimed at small to medium-sized businesses. The free tier will include basic task management and collaboration features, while the paid tier will offer advanced reporting, integrations, and unlimited projects.

**Candidate**: Thank you for that context. To estimate the conversion rate from free to paid users in the first six months, let's consider several factors that could influence this:

1. **Value Proposition**  
   * How compelling are the paid features compared to the free tier?  
   * What pain points do the paid features solve?  
2. **Target Market**  
   * How price-sensitive is our target market?  
   * What's the typical budget for project management tools in SMBs?  
3. **Competitive Landscape**  
   * How does our freemium model compare to competitors?  
   * What are typical conversion rates in our industry?  
4. **User Onboarding and Education**  
   * How effectively do we showcase the value of paid features?  
   * Do we have a clear upgrade path for users?  
5. **Pricing Strategy**  
   * How is our paid tier priced relative to the market?  
   * Do we offer different paid plans or just one?  
6. **Usage Patterns**  
   * How quickly do users hit the limitations of the free tier?  
   * What percentage of free users are power users who might need advanced features?

To structure our estimation, let's use a user journey map approach to identify potential conversion points:

1. **Sign-up**: Users create a free account  
2. **Basic Usage**: Users start using free features  
3. **Feature Exploration**: Users discover product capabilities  
4. **Team Collaboration**: Users invite team members  
5. **Advanced Needs**: Users require more sophisticated features  
6. **Decision Point**: Users evaluate upgrading to paid tier

Now, let's estimate the conversion rate based on this journey. I'll need some baseline data. Do we have information on:

1. Typical freemium conversion rates in the project management SaaS industry?  
2. Our expected number of free sign-ups in the first six months?  
3. Our pricing for the paid tier compared to competitors?

**Interviewer**: Let's work with assumptions for those numbers.

**Candidate**: Understood. I'll make some reasonable assumptions based on industry standards and the information provided:

1. Typical freemium conversion rates in SaaS: 2-5% overall, with project management tools often on the higher end due to clear business value  
2. Expected free sign-ups in first six months: 100,000 users  
3. Our pricing is competitive, slightly below the average for similar tools

Let's break down the conversion funnel for the first six months:

**Conservative Scenario:**

1. Sign-up to Basic Usage: 80% (80,000 users)  
2. Basic Usage to Feature Exploration: 50% (40,000 users)  
3. Feature Exploration to Team Collaboration: 30% (12,000 users)  
4. Team Collaboration to Advanced Needs: 25% (3,000 users)  
5. Advanced Needs to Paid Conversion: 60% (1,800 users)  
6. Total Conversion: 1,800 / 100,000 \= 1.8%

**Moderate Scenario:**

1. Sign-up to Basic Usage: 85% (85,000 users)  
2. Basic Usage to Feature Exploration: 60% (51,000 users)  
3. Feature Exploration to Team Collaboration: 40% (20,400 users)  
4. Team Collaboration to Advanced Needs: 35% (7,140 users)  
5. Advanced Needs to Paid Conversion: 70% (4,998 users)  
6. Total Conversion: 4,998 / 100,000 \= 5%

**Optimistic Scenario:**

1. Sign-up to Basic Usage: 90% (90,000 users)  
2. Basic Usage to Feature Exploration: 70% (63,000 users)  
3. Feature Exploration to Team Collaboration: 50% (31,500 users)  
4. Team Collaboration to Advanced Needs: 45% (14,175 users)  
5. Advanced Needs to Paid Conversion: 80% (11,340 users)  
6. Total Conversion: 11,340 / 100,000 \= 11.34%

Based on this analysis, I estimate that introducing a freemium model could result in a conversion rate of **1.8% to 11.34% in the first six months**, with a moderate estimate of **5%**.

**Insights from the journey-based breakdown:**

1. The biggest drop-offs occur in the early stages, highlighting the importance of user onboarding and quickly demonstrating value.  
2. Team collaboration is a critical stage for conversions, suggesting we should focus on multi-user features and team-based pricing.  
3. A significant portion of users who reach the Advanced Needs stage convert, indicating that our paid features are compelling for power users.

**Sanity Check:** Our moderate estimate of 5% aligns with the higher end of typical SaaS freemium conversion rates (2-5%). This makes sense for a project management tool with clear business value. The conservative estimate (1.8%) and optimistic estimate (11.34%) provide a reasonable range based on various factors that could influence conversion.

Is there any part of this estimation you'd like me to expand on or reconsider?

### **Why it Works**

This answer uses the GAME framework, demonstrates thoughtful analysis through user journey mapping, scenario planning, and sanity checking.

It showcases analytical thinking and product strategy skills valuable for product managers dealing with monetization questions.

## **4\. Performance and Scale**

### **Example: What effect on customer lifetime value might we see if we reduce our app's crash rate from 2% to 0.5%?Candidate's response:**

**Candidate**: Before we dive into the estimation, I'd like to clarify some details about our app and user base. Could you provide some context about the type of app we're dealing with, our current customer lifetime value (CLV), and the average subscription length?

**Interviewer**: Our app is a subscription-based fitness tracking application. The current average customer lifetime value is $120, and the average subscription length is 12 months.

**Candidate**: Thank you for that context. To estimate the effect on customer lifetime value from reducing our app's crash rate from 2% to 0.5%, let's consider the following factors:

1. User Experience Impact  
2. Retention Rate Improvement  
3. Word-of-Mouth Marketing  
4. Customer Support Cost Reduction

Let's break this down using a structured approach:

1. User Experience Impact:  
   * Current crash rate: 2% (2 crashes per 100 sessions)  
   * Improved crash rate: 0.5% (0.5 crashes per 100 sessions)  
   * Improvement: 1.5 percentage points or 75% reduction in crashes  
2. Retention Rate Improvement:  
   * Let's assume each crash has a small chance of causing a user to churn  
   * If 1% of crashes lead to churn, current additional churn due to crashes: 2% \* 1% \= 0.02%  
   * Improved additional churn due to crashes: 0.5% \* 1% \= 0.005%  
   * Churn reduction: 0.02% \- 0.005% \= 0.015%  
3. Word-of-Mouth Marketing:  
   * Assume each crash reduces the likelihood of recommendation by 0.1%  
   * Current negative impact: 2% \* 0.1% \= 0.2% reduction in recommendations  
   * Improved negative impact: 0.5% \* 0.1% \= 0.05% reduction in recommendations  
   * Improvement in recommendations: 0.2% \- 0.05% \= 0.15%  
4. Customer Support Cost:  
   * Assume 10% of crashes result in a support ticket  
   * Current support tickets due to crashes: 2% \* 10% \= 0.2% of sessions  
   * Improved support tickets due to crashes: 0.5% \* 10% \= 0.05% of sessions  
   * Reduction in support tickets: 0.2% \- 0.05% \= 0.15%

Now, let's calculate the impact on CLV:

Current CLV: $120 Average subscription length: 12 months Monthly value: $120 / 12 \= $10 per month

1. Retention Rate Improvement:  
   * Current monthly churn: 1 / 12 \= 8.33% (assuming uniform distribution)  
   * Improved monthly churn: 8.33% \- 0.015% \= 8.315%  
   * New average subscription length: 1 / 8.315% \= 12.03 months  
   * New CLV: 12.03 \* $10 \= $120.30  
2. Word-of-Mouth Marketing:  
   * Assume 5% of users refer one new user during their lifetime  
   * Current referral value: $120 \* 5% \= $6  
   * Improved referral value: $120 \* (5% \+ 0.15%) \= $6.18  
   * Increase in CLV due to referrals: $6.18 \- $6 \= $0.18  
3. Customer Support Cost:  
   * Assume support cost is 5% of CLV: $120 \* 5% \= $6  
   * Support cost reduction: $6 \* 0.15% \= $0.009

Total CLV Improvement: $120.30 (retention) \+ $0.18 (referrals) \+ $0.009 (support cost) \= $120.489

CLV Increase: $120.489 \- $120 \= $0.489 (0.41% increase)

Sanity Check:

* The estimated 0.41% increase in CLV seems reasonable given the relatively small change in crash rate (1.5 percentage points).  
* The largest impact comes from improved retention, which aligns with the importance of user experience in subscription-based apps.  
* The modest increase makes sense as crashes, while important, are just one factor in overall user satisfaction and retention.  
* To put it in perspective, this small percentage increase could be significant when applied to a large user base. For instance, with 1 million users, this would translate to an additional $489,000 in customer lifetime value.

To validate this estimate, I would suggest:

1. Analyzing historical data on user behavior and CLV for different app versions with varying crash rates.  
2. Conducting cohort analysis to compare retention rates between users who experience more crashes versus those who experience fewer.  
3. Surveying users to understand how app stability affects their satisfaction and likelihood to recommend or churn.

Is there any part of this estimation you'd like me to expand on or reconsider?

#### **Why it Works**

The candidate starts by clarifying important context, then uses a structured approach to break down the problem into measurable factors.

Each factor is tied mathematically to the crash rate reduction, showing logical reasoning and the ability to create models based on reasonable assumptions.

The detailed yet clear calculations, followed by a sanity check and validation suggestions, showcase strong quantitative skills and critical thinking.

1. How might reducing our app's load time from 5 seconds to 2 seconds impact our user retention rate?  
2. What could be the effect on user engagement if we optimize our app to use 30% less battery life?  
3. How many more concurrent users could our platform support if we implement a queue system for high-traffic periods?  
4. What impact on customer satisfaction could we expect if we reduce our average API response time from 500ms to 100ms?  
5. How might implementing offline mode capability affect our daily active user metrics?

10. What could be the impact on our Net Promoter Score if we reduce system downtime from 1% to 0.1%?

## **5\. User Retention and Satisfaction**

#### **Example: How much could we reduce customer churn by implementing a proactive customer success program?**

**Candidate**: Before we dive in, could you provide some context about our product and current churn rate?

**Interviewer**: We offer a B2B SaaS project management tool. Our current monthly churn rate is 5%, and we have 100,000 active customers.

**Candidate**: Thank you. I'd like to approach this by segmenting our churning customers based on engagement levels, estimating the program's reach and effectiveness for each segment, and then calculating the overall churn reduction. Does this approach sound reasonable to you?

**Interviewer**: Yes, that sounds like a good approach.

**Candidate**: Great. For segmentation, I'm thinking of categorizing churning customers into low, medium, and high engagement groups. Would you agree with this segmentation, or do you have a different preference?

**Interviewer**: That segmentation works. Please proceed.

**Candidate**: Thank you. Now, I'll need to make some assumptions about the segmentation breakdown and the program's effectiveness. May I state these assumptions and get your agreement before proceeding with the calculations?

**Interviewer**: Yes, go ahead.

**Candidate**: I'm considering the following assumptions:

1. Segmentation of churning customers:  
   * Low engagement (high risk): 50%  
   * Medium engagement: 30%  
   * High engagement (low risk): 20%  
2. Program reach: 60% of at-risk customers  
3. Program effectiveness:  
   * Low engagement: 5% reduction in churn  
   * Medium engagement: 10% reduction  
   * High engagement: 15% reduction

Do these assumptions seem reasonable to you?

**Interviewer**: Yes, those assumptions are reasonable for our analysis.

**Candidate**: Thank you. Now, let's calculate the potential churn reduction for three scenarios:

Conservative Scenario:

* Program reach: 50%  
* Effectiveness: 3% (low), 7% (medium), 10% (high)

Calculation:

* Low: 2,500 \* 50% \* 3% \= 38 customers saved  
* Medium: 1,500 \* 50% \* 7% \= 53 customers saved  
* High: 1,000 \* 50% \* 10% \= 50 customers saved Total saved: 38 \+ 53 \+ 50 \= 141 customers

New churn rate: (5,000 \- 141\) / 100,000 \= 4.86% Churn reduction: (5% \- 4.86%) / 5% \= 2.8%

Moderate Scenario:

* Program reach: 60%  
* Effectiveness: 5% (low), 10% (medium), 15% (high)

Calculation:

* Low: 2,500 \* 60% \* 5% \= 75 customers saved  
* Medium: 1,500 \* 60% \* 10% \= 90 customers saved  
* High: 1,000 \* 60% \* 15% \= 90 customers saved Total saved: 75 \+ 90 \+ 90 \= 255 customers

New churn rate: (5,000 \- 255\) / 100,000 \= 4.75% Churn reduction: (5% \- 4.75%) / 5% \= 5.1%

Optimistic Scenario:

* Program reach: 70%  
* Effectiveness: 7% (low), 13% (medium), 20% (high)

Calculation:

* Low: 2,500 \* 70% \* 7% \= 123 customers saved  
* Medium: 1,500 \* 70% \* 13% \= 137 customers saved  
* High: 1,000 \* 70% \* 20% \= 140 customers saved Total saved: 123 \+ 137 \+ 140 \= 400 customers

New churn rate: (5,000 \- 400\) / 100,000 \= 4.60% Churn reduction: (5% \- 4.60%) / 5% \= 8.0%

Based on these calculations, I estimate that implementing a proactive customer success program could reduce our customer churn by approximately:

* Conservative scenario: 2.8% reduction (new churn rate: 4.86%)  
* Moderate scenario: 5.1% reduction (new churn rate: 4.75%)  
* Optimistic scenario: 8.0% reduction (new churn rate: 4.60%)

Sanity check: Let's consider this estimate in context. A 5.1% reduction in churn (our moderate scenario) means we're saving about 255 customers per month from churning. For a B2B SaaS product with 100,000 customers, this seems reasonable. It's a meaningful improvement without being unrealistically high.

Moreover, if we assume an average customer lifetime value of $1,000, this churn reduction would translate to about $255,000 in preserved revenue per month or $3 million annually. This could justify a significant investment in a customer success program while still providing a positive ROI.

In conclusion, while the impact may seem modest, a 2.8% to 8% reduction in churn rate can have a substantial effect on our business over time. However, to validate these estimates and maximize the program's effectiveness, we should consider running a pilot program with a subset of our customers and closely monitor the results before full implementation.

Would you like me to expand on any part of this analysis or discuss how we might validate these estimates?

#### **Why It Works**

The candidate clarifies context, proposes a methodology, and seeks agreement on assumptions before diving into calculations.

The use of multiple scenarios shows nuanced thinking, while the sanity check demonstrates business acumen by relating the results to real-world implications.

Overall, the response balances analytical rigor with practical business considerations, reflecting the comprehensive thinking essential in effective product management.

#### **Additional Practice Questions**

1. How might reducing our app's average load time from 3 seconds to 1 second impact our 30-day retention rate?  
2. What improvement in Net Promoter Score could we expect by implementing a 24/7 live chat support feature?  
3. How much could we increase our free-to-paid conversion rate by introducing a limited-time trial of premium features?  
4. What effect on user engagement might we see if we implement a personalized content recommendation system?  
5. How could introducing a loyalty program impact our customer lifetime value?  
6. What reduction in customer support tickets might we achieve by improving our app's onboarding process?  
7. How might implementing a referral program affect our customer acquisition cost and retention rate?  
8. What impact on user satisfaction could we expect by reducing our average response time to customer inquiries from 24 hours to 4 hours?  
9. How could gamifying certain aspects of our app affect daily active user metrics?  
10. What improvement in annual renewal rates might we see by implementing a proactive feature education program for our SaaS product?

### **6\. Market Sizing Questions**

#### **6.1 Size the market for electric vehicles in the US in 2030**

**Candidate**: Before we dive into the estimation, could you provide some context about what specific aspects of the electric vehicle market we're focusing on? Are we looking at annual sales, total market value, or something else?

**Interviewer**: Let's focus on the annual sales value of electric vehicles in the US in 2030\.

**Candidate**: Thank you for clarifying. I'd like to approach this by estimating the total car market size, then the EV market share, and finally calculating the annual sales value. Does this approach sound reasonable to you?

**Interviewer**: Yes, that sounds like a good approach.

**Candidate**: Great. I'll need to make some assumptions about population growth, car ownership rates, EV adoption, and average EV prices. May I state these assumptions and get your agreement before proceeding with the calculations?

**Interviewer**: Yes, go ahead.

**Candidate**: I'm considering the following assumptions:

1. US population in 2030: 350 million (assuming slight growth from current \~330 million)  
2. Cars per capita: 0.8 (accounting for urban areas with lower car ownership)  
3. Average car lifespan: 12 years  
4. EV market share of new car sales in 2030: 15-30% (range for different scenarios)  
5. Average EV price in 2030: $35,000-$45,000 (range accounting for different scenarios)

Do these assumptions seem reasonable to you?

**Interviewer**: Yes, those assumptions are reasonable for our analysis.

**Candidate**: Thank you. Now, let's calculate the market size for three scenarios:

1. Total cars in the US in 2030: 350 million \* 0.8 \= 280 million cars  
2. Annual car sales (assuming replacement rate of 1/12 due to 12-year lifespan): 280 million / 12 \= 23.33 million cars per year

**Conservative Scenario:**

* EV market share: 15%  
* Average EV price: $45,000  
* Annual EV sales: 23.33 million \* 15% \= 3.5 million EVs  
* Market value: 3.5 million \* $45,000 \= $157.5 billion

**Moderate Scenario:**

* EV market share: 22%  
* Average EV price: $40,000  
* Annual EV sales: 23.33 million \* 22% \= 5.13 million EVs  
* Market value: 5.13 million \* $40,000 \= $205.2 billion

**Optimistic Scenario:**

* EV market share: 30%  
* Average EV price: $35,000  
* Annual EV sales: 23.33 million \* 30% \= 7 million EVs  
* Market value: 7 million \* $35,000 \= $245 billion

Based on these calculations, I estimate that the annual sales value of the electric vehicle market in the US in 2030 will be between $157.5 billion and $245 billion, with a moderate estimate of $205.2 billion.

Would you like me to expand on any part of this analysis or discuss how we might further validate these estimates?

#### **Why it Works**

This answer demonstrates key product management skills through its structured approach and data-driven analysis. The candidate clarifies context, proposes a methodology, and seeks agreement on assumptions before diving into calculations.

The use of multiple scenarios shows nuanced thinking, while the sanity check demonstrates business acumen by relating the results to current market data.

#### **Additional Practice Questions**

1. Estimate the number of electric vehicles that will be on US roads by 2035\.  
2. What could be the total revenue of the global video game industry in 2028?  
3. How many smart home devices might be in use in European households by 2030?  
4. Estimate the number of plant-based meat alternative meals consumed in the US in a week by 2032\.  
5. What might be the total market value for telehealth services in North America by 2029?

10. What might be the total data storage capacity used for cloud computing services worldwide in 2030?

## **Part 4: Presenting Your Estimate and Handling Follow-ups**

How you present your estimate can be just as important as the calculation itself. Let's explore how to communicate your results effectively and handle interviewer follow-ups.

### **4.1 Presenting Your Estimate**

When you've reached your final number, don't just blurt it out. Frame your answer thoughtfully.

#### **Recap Your Approach**

Briefly summarize the key steps in your estimation. This reminds the interviewer of your structured thinking.

"To estimate the number of pizzas sold daily in New York City, I considered the population, percentage likely to order pizza, frequency of orders, and average pizzas per order."

#### **State Your Estimate Clearly**

Provide your estimate in a clear, confident manner. Use round numbers for easier comprehension.

"Based on these factors, I estimate that approximately 500,000 pizzas are sold daily in New York City."

#### **Acknowledge Uncertainty**

No estimation is perfect. Acknowledge this to show self-awareness.

"Given the assumptions made, this number could reasonably range from 400,000 to 600,000 pizzas."

#### **Offer Contextual Comparisons**

Help the interviewer grasp the scale of your estimate by offering comparisons.

"This means about one in every 16 New Yorkers is ordering a pizza each day, which seems reasonable given the city's food culture."

### **4.2 Handling Follow-up Questions**

Interviewers often ask follow-up questions to test your flexibility and deeper understanding. Here's how to handle them.

#### **Stay Calm**

Follow-ups aren't meant to trip you up. They're opportunities to showcase your thinking.

Take a breath. It's okay to pause before answering.

#### **Listen Carefully**

Make sure you understand the question. If unsure, ask for clarification.

"Just to confirm, are you asking how the estimate would change if we considered only weekends?"

#### **Adjust Your Model**

Show how your estimate would change based on new information or assumptions.

"If we focus only on weekends, I'd adjust the daily consumption up by about 30%. This would increase our estimate to around 650,000 pizzas per day on weekends."

#### **Discuss Implications**

Don't just recalculate. Discuss what the changes mean for the broader context.

"This weekend increase suggests pizza shops might need to staff up significantly for Friday and Saturday nights."

### **4.3 Common Follow-up Scenarios**

Here are some typical follow-up scenarios and how to handle them:

#### **Scenario 1: Challenging an Assumption**

**Interviewer**: "You assumed 25% of our users would engage with the new feature daily. What if it's only 10%?"

Your approach:

1. Acknowledge the change  
2. Quickly recalculate  
3. Discuss product implications

"If only 10% engage daily, our overall engagement increase would be lower, around 8-12% instead of 20-30%. This might suggest that we need to focus more on feature discovery and user education. We could consider implementing user onboarding tutorials or push notifications to drive awareness and adoption of the new feature."

#### **Scenario 2: Exploring Edge Cases**

**Interviewer**: "How would your estimate change during a major event, like the Olympics?"

Your approach:

1. Consider the event's impact on user behavior  
2. Make new assumptions  
3. Revise your estimate  
4. Discuss product strategy implications

"During a major event like the Olympics, we might see overall engagement increase by 40-50% as users check for updates more frequently. Our personalized recommendation system could be even more valuable during this time, helping users discover content they're most interested in amid the surge of event-related content. We might want to consider creating an event-specific version of our algorithm to capitalize on this opportunity."

#### **Scenario 3: Linking to Monetization**

**Interviewer**: "Based on your engagement estimate, how might this impact our ad revenue?"

Your approach:

1. Connect engagement to ad impressions  
2. Make assumptions about ad rates  
3. Calculate potential revenue increase  
4. Discuss broader monetization strategy

*"If we're seeing 20-30% more engagement, we could potentially show 20-30% more ads. Assuming our current average revenue per user (ARPU) is $2 per month from ads, this could increase to $2.40-$2.60. For our user base of 10 million, this translates to an additional $4-6 million in monthly ad revenue. However, we should be cautious about increasing ad load too much, as it might negatively impact user experience. We could also explore alternative monetization strategies, like premium features, that leverage the increased engagement."*

#### **Scenario 4: Technical Feasibility**

**Interviewer**: "What technical challenges might we face in implementing this personalized recommendation system?"

Your approach:

1. Consider infrastructure requirements  
2. Discuss data and privacy implications  
3. Think about scalability  
4. Mention potential algorithmic challenges

"Implementing a personalized recommendation system would require significant data processing capabilities. We'd need to ensure our infrastructure can handle real-time analysis of user behavior. There are also data privacy considerations – we'd need to be transparent about data usage and comply with regulations like GDPR. Scalability could be a challenge as our user base grows. Additionally, developing an algorithm that provides relevant recommendations while avoiding 'filter bubbles' would require ongoing refinement and possibly AI/ML expertise."

#### **Scenario 5: User Segments**

**Interviewer**: "How might the impact of this feature vary across different user segments?"

Your approach:

1. Identify key user segments  
2. Discuss how each segment might interact with the feature  
3. Estimate varying impacts  
4. Suggest segment-specific strategies

"We might see different impacts across user segments. Power users, who make up 20% of our base but drive 60% of engagement, might see a 40-50% engagement increase as they're more likely to interact with and benefit from personalized recommendations. Casual users might only see a 10-15% increase. New users could see a 30-35% increase as the feature helps them discover relevant content quickly, potentially improving our activation rates. Based on this, we might want to tailor our rollout strategy, perhaps focusing on new user onboarding and retention of casual users, while using power users for beta testing and feedback."

### **4.4 Final Tips**

Remember, the goal of estimation questions in PM interviews isn't just to reach a number. It's to demonstrate your product thinking process, business acumen, and ability to make data-driven decisions.

1. Always tie your estimates back to user value and business impact.  
2. Show that you understand the balance between user needs, business goals, and technical feasibility.  
3. Be prepared to discuss the broader product strategy implications of your estimates.  
4. Demonstrate your ability to prioritize by discussing which metrics or outcomes are most important in each scenario.  
5. Show adaptability by being willing to adjust your approach based on new information or constraints.  
6. Don't be afraid to discuss potential risks or downsides – it shows you're thinking holistically about product decisions.

With practice and the strategies outlined in this guide, you'll be well-prepared to tackle any estimation question that comes your way in your product management interviews. Good luck\!

---

## **Postscript: A Critical Look at Estimation Questions in PM Interviews**

While we've spent this guide exploring how to excel at estimation questions, it's worth examining their place in the PM interview process.

### **The Popularity Paradox**

Estimation questions remain popular in PM interviews. They're easy to administer and seem to test analytical skills.

But their prevalence doesn't necessarily equate to effectiveness.

### **Limited Scope**

These questions often focus on a narrow set of skills. They primarily test quick math and basic market sizing.

However, product management requires a much broader skill set. Creativity, user empathy, and strategic thinking are equally crucial.

### **Artificial Pressure**

The time-pressured nature of these questions creates an artificial environment. It doesn't reflect the realities of day-to-day PM work.

In practice, PMs often have time to research, consult data, and collaborate with teams.

### **Potential for Bias**

Estimation questions can favor candidates from certain backgrounds. Those with consulting experience or specific industry knowledge might have an unfair advantage.

This could lead to overlooking diverse talent with valuable, non-traditional perspectives.

### **Missing the Mark**

Perhaps most importantly, these questions often fail to assess key PM competencies. They don't test a candidate's ability to:

1. Understand user needs  
2. Prioritize features  
3. Collaborate with cross-functional teams  
4. Make data-driven decisions

### **A Better Approach**

While estimation questions have their place, they shouldn't be the cornerstone of PM interviews.

Interviewers would do better to focus on:

1. Case studies that reflect real product challenges  
2. Discussions about past projects and decision-making processes  
3. Collaborative exercises that mimic actual PM work

These approaches can provide a more holistic view of a candidate's potential as a PM.

### **The Bottom Line**

Estimation questions can be a useful tool in the interview toolkit. But they shouldn't be overemphasized.

The best PM interviews assess a wide range of skills and simulate real-world scenarios. They look beyond mere number crunching to evaluate a candidate's full potential as a product leader.

As the field of product management evolves, so too should our interview processes. It's time to reconsider the weight we give to estimation questions and explore more comprehensive evaluation methods.

## **The Interview That Changed Everything**

# **Let's start with the question that stumped Sarah in her mock interview:**

# ***"Amazon just announced unlimited free photo storage. You're the PM of Google Photos. What would you do?"***

# **Here's how Sarah initially approached it:**

# **Sarah: "Let me use the Strategy Triangle framework to break this down. For 'Where to Play,' we should look at our target market—"** 

# 

# **Interviewer: "Before we jump into frameworks, what do you think is the core strategic challenge here?"** 

# 

# **Sarah: "Um... well, the framework helps us identify—"** 

# 

# **Interviewer: "Let's take a step back. What's your initial gut reaction to this news about Amazon?"**

# **This exchange reveals the first crucial lesson: The interviewer doesn't want to see you apply frameworks. *They want to see how you think*.**

# ***Here's how Sarah eventually learned to approach the same question:***

# **Sarah: "Before I dive into a response, I'd like to understand what this move signals about Amazon's strategy. They're clearly using photos as a wedge into consumer cloud storage, likely to drive Prime adoption. This raises interesting questions about how we at Google Photos should position ourselves. Are we competing on storage, or are we solving a deeper user need? What unique advantages do we have in the Google ecosystem? And most importantly, what's our belief about where photo management is heading in the next 5-10 years?"** 

# 

# **Interviewer: "Interesting perspective. Tell me more about where you think photo management is heading."**

# **Notice the difference? Instead of reaching for a framework, Sarah started with strategic questions that demonstrated her ability to:**

1. # **Read competitive moves**

2. # **Think about ecosystem advantages**

3. # **Consider long-term market evolution**

## **The Three Shifts That Transform Strategic Thinking**

# **Through coaching Sarah and dozens of other candidates, I've identified three key mental shifts that separate good from great strategic thinkers:**

### **1\. Solutions ➜ Systems**

# **Most candidates jump straight to solutions. Great candidates first map the ecosystem. Here's how Sarah learned to do this:**

# **Instead of immediately responding to Amazon's move, she drew out the entire photo storage ecosystem:**

* # **Users (casual vs. professional)**

* # **Storage providers (cloud companies, device manufacturers)**

* # **Adjacent services (editing tools, social sharing)**

* # **Technology trends (AI/ML, mobile capabilities)**

* # **Business models (free, freemium, premium)**

# **This systems view helped her spot opportunities others missed.**

### **2\. Features ➜ First Principles**

# **Average candidates think in terms of features and countermoves.**

# **Great candidates *go back to first principles*. When analyzing Google Photos' position, Sarah learned to ask:**

* # **What fundamental user needs drive photo storage and management?**

* # **What unique capabilities does Google have that others can't easily replicate?**

* # **What core beliefs about the future are we betting on?**

### **3\. Tactical ➜ Transformational**

# **Most candidates play defense, reacting to competitive moves.**

# **The best candidates see opportunities for transformation.**

# **Sarah's winning response wasn't about matching Amazon's storage offer—it was about redefining what photo management could be.**
